tip.title: Je voudrais … — and what you get
tip.body: Je voudrais (I would like) is the polite way to order; Je vais prendre … (I'll have …) works too. Every noun is masculine or feminine: un café, un thé, but une bière, une carafe d'eau. Un café is a small espresso; un crème is a coffee with hot frothed milk. Une carafe d'eau is a jug of tap water — free with a meal in French restaurants, and usually given for free in cafés too. Voudrais sounds like "voo-dray": the final -s is silent.

tip.title: L'addition and service compris
tip.body: In France the waiter won't bring the bill until you ask: L'addition, s'il vous plaît ! To get attention, say S'il vous plaît ! or Excusez-moi — calling "Garçon !" is old-fashioned and sounds rude. Service is included in the prices (service compris), so a tip is a small optional extra: round up or leave a few coins. Addition starts with a vowel, so la becomes l': l'addition.

tip.title: Bonjour first, then your bread
tip.body: Always start with Bonjour ! before you order — skipping it is considered rude. Une baguette is the classic loaf; une tradition (baguette de tradition) is made to a stricter traditional recipe and is a favourite of many locals. Bakers often ask Et avec ceci ? (anything else?); answer Ce sera tout (that's all). Croissant ends in a nasal vowel: the -t is silent.

lessons.title: un, une, des & le, la, les
lessons.goal: Use the right article with café words.

tip.title: a / some vs the
tip.body: Un (masc.) and une (fem.) mean "a": un café, une bière. The plural is des ("some") — and French can't drop it the way English drops "some": des croissants. Le (masc.), la (fem.) and les (plural) mean "the": le café, la baguette, les croissants. Before a vowel or silent h, le and la become l': l'eau, l'addition. Les and des link with a "z" before a vowel: les_oranges, des_œufs. Learn every noun with its article!

culture.title: Café life — and the chocolatine debate
culture.body: In a French café you can sit for a long time over a single coffee; nobody will rush you. A coffee drunk standing at the counter (au comptoir) is often cheaper than one served at a table or on the terrace. In south-western France — and in Québec — a pain au chocolat is called une chocolatine, a friendly and never-ending debate between French regions. In Belgium you may hear une couque au chocolat.
